Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:S^{d-1}\to S^{d-1}$ be a homeomorphism of the unit
sphere $S^{d-1}\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Then $f$ extends to a homeomorphism
$F:D^d\to D^d$ of the closed unit disk, given by
$$F(0)=0,\qquad F(rx)=r\,f(x)\quad\text{for }0<r\le1,\ x\in S^{d-1}.$$
The extension need not be smooth at the origin.

derivations.claim: Let $c((e^{i\theta},w),s)=((1-s/8)e^{i\theta},w)$ for $(e^{i\theta},w)\in\partial V'$ and $s\in[0,2]$; this is a collar because its radial coordinate ranges from $1$ to $3/4$. Set $\rho(s)=1-s$ for $0\le s\le1$ and $\rho(s)=0$ for $1\le s\le2$. The map $J(c(x,s))=c(H_{\rho(s)}(x),s)$ on the collar, extended by the identity outside it, is a homeomorphism: its inverse replaces $H_{\rho(s)}$ with $H_{\rho(s)}^{-1}$. It restricts to $H_1$ at the boundary and is isotopic to the identity through the same formula with $H_{u\rho(s)}$ for $u\in[0,1]$. Thus $h_0=J|_{\partial V'}\circ h$ sends $\mu$ exactly to $\mu'$, and extending $h_0$ suffices because postcomposition with $J^{-1}$ recovers an extension of $h$ without changing its orientation sign.

Cut $V$ and $V'$ along the product meridian disks $D=D^2\times\{1\}$ and $D'=D^2\times\{1\}$. Each cut-open solid torus is $D^2\times[0,1]$. After centering the interval at $0$, this convex cylinder is homeomorphic to the unit ball by radial rescaling: in direction $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in S^2$ its boundary radius is $R(u)=\min\{(u_1^2+u_2^2)^{-1/2},(2|u_3|)^{-1}\}$, with a zero denominator interpreted as $+\infty$, and $(r,u)\mapsto rR(u)u$ gives the homeomorphism. The boundary of each cut-open torus consists of the annulus obtained by cutting the boundary torus along the meridian and two disk faces. The restriction of $h_0$ maps the annular portions to one another. Its common restriction to $\mu$ extends over each disk face by [F1], using the same disk map on both copies. The radial disk maps send the center of each disk face to the center of its target face. These maps assemble to a homeomorphism $\psi:\partial B\to\partial B'$ between the sphere boundaries of the cut-open balls, carrying the pair of disk-face centers to that pair in the target.

Identify each cut-open ball with the unit ball in $\mathbb R^3$. Apply [F1] with $d=3$ to extend $\psi$ radially over the ball. The cylinder-to-ball radial rescaling of step 2.1 carries the central product arc $\{0\}\times[0,1]$ to the diameter joining the two disk-face center points. Since $\psi$ carries those endpoints to the target pair, its radial extension carries this entire diameter to the corresponding target diameter. Thus the ball extension preserves the product core arc. The extension has orientation sign equal to the degree sign of $\psi$. On the open annulus away from the disk faces, $\psi$ is exactly $h_0$; cutting does not change the local boundary orientation there, so this degree sign is the orientation sign of $h_0$.

The two copies of each meridian disk receive the same disk map from [F1], so the ball extension agrees on their identified faces. It therefore descends after regluing to a homeomorphism $V\to V'$ extending $h_0$ and carrying the product core circle to the target core circle. Composing with $J^{-1}$ extends the original $h$; this collar-supported map fixes the core and keeps the same orientation sign because $J$ is isotopic to the identity.

citations.quote: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

derivations.claim: Applying [F2] to the three crossing triples gives $a=bcb^{-1}$, $b=cac^{-1}$, and $c=aba^{-1}$. Substitute the third equation into the first to obtain $a=baba^{-1}b^{-1}$; right multiplication by $ba$ gives $aba=bab$. Under this relation, $cac^{-1}=aba^{-1}aab^{-1}a^{-1}=abab^{-1}a^{-1}=bab b^{-1}a^{-1}=b$, so the second crossing equation follows. Therefore eliminating $c$ from the presentation in [F1] yields exactly $\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$.
In the abelianization, the relation becomes $2[a]+[b]=[a]+2[b]$, hence $[a]=[b]$. The abelianization is the free abelian group on $[a],[b]$ modulo this single relation, so it is $\mathbb Z$.

Map $a\mapsto(12)$ and $b\mapsto(23)$ in $S_3$. Both $aba$ and $bab$ map to $(13)$, so the relation is satisfied. These two transpositions generate $S_3$, making the homomorphism surjective. Since $S_3$ is nonabelian, its surjective preimage $G_T$ is nonabelian.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere with a chosen connected exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K$. Let $(\mu,\lambda)$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude, assume $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, and assume $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ and $[\lambda]=0$. For coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero, let $E_K(p/q)$ be the filling whose attached solid-torus meridian maps to $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Then
$$H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z,&p\ne0,\\[2pt]\mathbb Z,&p=0.\end{cases}$$

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot, and let $p,q$ be coprime integers with $|p|=1$ and $q\ne0$. For the Dehn filling $Y_{p/q}=E_K(p/q)$ whose attached solid-torus meridian is identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ admits a homomorphism to $SU(2)$ with noncyclic image.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [A1], the countable-choice hypothesis of [F1] follows from [L1]. If $p=0$, [F1] gives $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. If $|p|\ge2$, it gives the nonzero finite group $\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$. In either case [F2] makes $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)$ a quotient of $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$, so the fundamental group is nontrivial.

If $|p|=1$, the nonmeridional condition gives $q\ne0$, and [F3] supplies a homomorphism with noncyclic image. The trivial group has only the trivial, hence cyclic, image, so $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

derivations.claim: Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F1] by [L1]. If $E_K(p/q)\cong S^3$, its first homology vanishes. By [F1], this excludes $p=0$ and every $|p|\ge2$, leaving $|p|=1$.

If additionally $q\ne0$, the slope is nonmeridional, so [F2] gives a nontrivial fundamental group, contradicting $\pi_1(S^3)=1$. Hence $q=0$; coprimality then gives $p=\pm1$, which is the meridional slope.

Conversely, if $q=0$, coprimality forces $p=\pm1$. By [F3], filling along this meridian slope is the original decomposition $S^3=E_K\cup N(K)$ up to the permitted solid-torus gluing, hence is homeomorphic to $S^3$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot and let $p,q$ be coprime integers, not both zero. The Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$ if and only if $q=0$, in which case $p=\pm1$ and the slope is the meridional slope $1/0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $S\subseteq N$ be a closed embedded submanifold, let $
u(S)$ be its normal bundle ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]), and let $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:\Omega	o N$ be two tubular neighbourhood embeddings of the same open disc bundle $\Omega=D(
u(S))$ whose restrictions to the zero section are the inclusion of $S$ ([[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Assume that $d\Phi_1$ and $d\Phi_2$ induce the same isomorphism from each vertical fibre $
u(S)_p$ to the ambient normal quotient $T_pN/T_pS$. (The usual normalization makes both induced maps the identity; merely fixing the zero section is insufficient.) Then, after shrinking $\Omega$ around the zero section, the two embeddings are isotopic through tubular neighbourhood embeddings fixing $S$ pointwise. Consequently, for every compact $A\subseteq S$ there is an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, compact support, $H_t\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$ (in particular $H_1\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_2$ there), and $H_t$ fixing a neighbourhood of $A$ in $S$ pointwise; when $S$ is compact one may take $A=S$ and obtain the agreement on a neighbourhood of all of $S$, with support in any prescribed neighbourhood of $\Phi_1(\Omega)\cup\Phi_2(\Omega)$.

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means

smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the

embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other

summands, and the number of components is $k$.

point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Suppose one knot is unknotted. By [F4] its standard radius-tube exterior is a solid torus with the displayed proper meridian disk. Use the ambient isotopy in the definition of unknotted to transport its chosen tube to a tube around the standard core $U$. Identify the transported and standard tube domains with the same normal bundle $
u(U)$. For each tubular embedding $\Phi_j$, its differential along the zero section induces an invertible smooth bundle map $L_j:
u(U)	o
u(U)$ on the normal quotient: invertibility follows because $\Phi_j$ is an embedding and is the identity on the zero section. Precompose $\Phi_j$ with the fibrewise map $L_j^{-1}$. After restricting to a common neighbourhood of the zero section, both induced normal maps are the identity; compactness of $U$ lets us choose one such neighbourhood for the whole core. Thus the hypotheses of [F5] hold. Under [A1], [L1] supplies its countable-choice premise, so an ambient isotopy identifies the tubes after shrinking. The standard disk transfers to the smaller chosen exterior. By [F6], the region between the smaller and original tube is a product boundary collar; trim or extend the disk across the product annulus so its boundary lies on the chosen exterior torus. The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pulling that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ preserves proper embedding and essential boundary, giving a compressing disk in the other exterior, contrary to [F2]. Thus either both are unknotted or both are nontrivial.

Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. If $h$ preserves orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,w)$; if $h$ reverses orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,\overline w)$. In either case $g$ has the same orientation sign as $h$ and sends the source meridian to the target meridian. If $\phi:\partial W\to\partial E_K$ is the source gluing map, define the target gluing map by $\phi'=h\circ\phi\circ g^{-1}$. It is orientation-reversing because $\phi$ is and $g,h$ have the same sign; its meridian image is $h(\mu_K)$, so it defines the filling along $\gamma$. The maps $h$ and $g$ glue to a homeomorphism of the filled manifolds. The source filling is $S^3$, hence the target filling along $\gamma$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$. By [F1], $\gamma$ is the target meridian slope; [F7] then gives the boundary isotopy in the Statement.

If both are unknotted, [F8] gives ambient equivalences from each knot to the standard unknot; composing them gives an ambient equivalence between the knots. This conclusion is independent of whether the given $h$ preserves the knot-meridian slope.

Apply [F3] to the actual boundary restriction of $h$ and the two tubular solid tori. The extensions agree with $h$ on the common boundary and therefore glue to a homeomorphism of pairs $(S^3,K)\to(S^3,K')$. By [F3] the ambient orientation sign is the same as that of $h$. Together with steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 this proves every case.

derivations.claim: The matrix $A$ is integral with determinant $1$, so its linear map on $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ is a torus homeomorphism. Its first column is $(1,0)$, hence it sends $\mu$ to $\mu$, and its second column is $(2,1)$, hence it sends $\lambda$ to $2\mu+\lambda$.

Define $F:V\to V$ by $F(z,w)=(w^2z,w)$. Since $|w|=1$, this maps $D^2\times S^1$ to itself, and its inverse is $(z',w')\mapsto((w')^{-2}z',w')$. Thus $F$ is a homeomorphism. On the meridian it has degree $1$; on the longitude it winds twice in the disk angle and once in the circle coordinate, giving the same matrix $A$.

The disk rotation $z\mapsto w^2z$ varies continuously with $w$ and contributes no orientation reversal; the circle coordinate is unchanged. Hence $F$ preserves the product orientation and is the required extension. This also instantiates [F1].

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

derivations.claim: The crossing-free unknot diagram has one under-arc and no crossings. By [F1] its group presentation has one generator and no relators, so every reduced word is a power of that generator and $\pi_1(S^3\setminus U)\cong\mathbb Z$. By [F2] the trefoil group is nonabelian, hence it is not isomorphic to the unknot group. If $U$ and $T$ were ambient equivalent, [F4] and [F5] would give an isomorphism of their complement groups. Therefore they are not ambient equivalent.

Under [A1], the homology supplier [F3] applies to both knots. Each abelianized peripheral system has $H_1\cong\mathbb Z$ with the meridian as generator and preferred longitude zero. The isomorphism sending $[\mu_U]$ to $[\mu_T]$ therefore sends the complete decorated triple $(H_1,[\mu],[\lambda])$ for $U$ to that for $T$. The systems agree although the knots do not, refuting the assertion.
